## Part A: Queries

```{=html}
<p>These use only SQL from the Week 2 and Week 3 lectures. Try each question yourself before reading the query.</p>
```

### Example 1: Highest-paid instructor in each department

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> For every department, find the instructor(s) with the highest salary in that department.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: correlated subquery, aggregate in a subquery</div>
```

```sql
select i.dept_name, i.name, i.salary
from instructor as i
where i.salary = (select max(j.salary)
                  from instructor as j
                  where j.dept_name = i.dept_name)
order by i.salary desc;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>dept_name</th><th>name</th><th>salary</th></tr><tr><td>Pol. Sci.</td><td>Wieland</td><td>124651.41</td></tr><tr><td>Physics</td><td>Voronina</td><td>121141.99</td></tr><tr><td>Marketing</td><td>Mird</td><td>119921.41</td></tr><tr><td>English</td><td>Sakurai</td><td>118143.98</td></tr><tr><td>Cybernetics</td><td>Bietzk</td><td>117836.50</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">First 5 of 17 rows shown</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">For each outer row i</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>take instructor i</b></div><span>e.g. Shuming, Physics</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>inner query</b></div><span>max salary in Physics = 121141.99</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>compare</b></div><span>108011.81 = 121141.99? no → drop</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>next row</b></div><span>Voronina: equal → keep</span></div></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> The inner query uses <code>i.dept_name</code> from the outer row, so it is re-run for every instructor. 17 rows: one per department that has instructors. If two instructors shared the top salary, both would be listed.<br><b>Common mistake:</b> <code>select dept_name, name, max(salary) from instructor group by dept_name;</code> fails with <code>column "instructor.name" must appear in the GROUP BY clause</code>, because one group has many names.</div>
```

### Example 2: Departments paying above average

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> List departments whose average instructor salary is higher than the average salary of all instructors (77600.19).</div><div class="concept">Concepts: group by, having with a subquery</div>
```

```sql
select dept_name, round(avg(salary), 2) as avg_salary
from instructor
group by dept_name
having avg(salary) > (select avg(salary) from instructor)
order by avg_salary desc;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>dept_name</th><th>avg_salary</th></tr><tr><td>Physics</td><td>114576.90</td></tr><tr><td>Finance</td><td>105311.38</td></tr><tr><td>Pol. Sci.</td><td>100053.07</td></tr><tr><td>Geology</td><td>99382.59</td></tr><tr><td>Comp. Sci.</td><td>98133.47</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">First 5 of 9 rows shown</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>where</code> cannot contain <code>avg(salary)</code> because it filters single rows before grouping; <code>having</code> filters whole groups after <code>group by</code>. The subquery is not correlated: it is computed once (77600.19) and every group is compared with it.</div>
```

### Example 3: Second-highest salary

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Find the instructor with the second-highest salary, without using limit.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: nested subqueries, max of a filtered set</div>
```

```sql
select name, dept_name, salary
from instructor
where salary = (select max(salary)
                from instructor
                where salary < (select max(salary) from instructor));
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th><th>dept_name</th><th>salary</th></tr><tr><td>Voronina</td><td>Physics</td><td>121141.99</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Inside out</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>innermost</b></div><span>max = 124651.41 (Wieland)</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>middle</b></div><span>max of salaries &lt; 124651.41 = 121141.99</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>outer</b></div><span>who earns 121141.99? Voronina</span></div></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> Removing the highest value and taking the max of what is left gives the second-highest <i>value</i>. If two instructors tied for first place, this still returns the next lower salary, which <code>order by salary desc limit 1 offset 1</code> would not.</div>
```

### Example 4: Fall vs Spring sections per year

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> For each year, show the number of sections offered in Fall, in Spring, and in total, as one row per year.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: conditional aggregation: case inside sum</div>
```

```sql
select year,
       sum(case when semester = 'Fall'   then 1 else 0 end) as fall,
       sum(case when semester = 'Spring' then 1 else 0 end) as spring,
       count(*) as total
from section
group by year
order by year;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>year</th><th>fall</th><th>spring</th><th>total</th></tr><tr><td>2001</td><td>2</td><td>3</td><td>5</td></tr><tr><td>2002</td><td>9</td><td>4</td><td>13</td></tr><tr><td>2003</td><td>6</td><td>6</td><td>12</td></tr><tr><td>2004</td><td>3</td><td>4</td><td>7</td></tr><tr><td>2005</td><td>4</td><td>4</td><td>8</td></tr><tr><td>2006</td><td>8</td><td>5</td><td>13</td></tr><tr><td>2007</td><td>6</td><td>6</td><td>12</td></tr><tr><td>2008</td><td>1</td><td>9</td><td>10</td></tr><tr><td>2009</td><td>7</td><td>2</td><td>9</td></tr><tr><td>2010</td><td>5</td><td>6</td><td>11</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(10 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> Each section row adds 1 to exactly one of the two <code>case</code> sums. Turning row values (Fall, Spring) into columns this way is called a <b>pivot</b>.</div>
```

### Example 5: Courses that are prerequisites of each other

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Find pairs of courses where each course is a prerequisite of the other (a cycle in <code>prereq</code>).</div><div class="concept">Concepts: self join with two conditions, removing mirrored pairs</div>
```

```sql
select p1.course_id, p1.prereq_id
from prereq as p1 join prereq as p2
     on p1.prereq_id = p2.course_id
    and p2.prereq_id = p1.course_id
order by p1.course_id;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>course_id</th><th>prereq_id</th></tr><tr><td>133</td><td>852</td></tr><tr><td>634</td><td>864</td></tr><tr><td>852</td><td>133</td></tr><tr><td>864</td><td>634</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(4 rows)</div>
<p>Each pair appears twice, once from each side. Keep one copy by adding <code>where p1.course_id &lt; p1.prereq_id</code>:</p><div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>course_id</th><th>prereq_id</th></tr><tr><td>133</td><td>852</td></tr><tr><td>634</td><td>864</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(2 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> Aliases <code>p1</code> and <code>p2</code> let one table play two roles. Row (133, 852) in p1 matches row (852, 133) in p2. The dataset really contains these cycles, so no student could ever satisfy the prerequisites of courses 133, 852, 634 or 864.</div>
```

### Example 6: Goal difference table

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> For each team, show goals scored, goals conceded and goal difference across all its home and away matches, best goal difference first.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: subquery in from, union all, join, group by, expression in order by</div>
```

```sql
select t.name,
       sum(r.gf)            as scored,
       sum(r.ga)            as conceded,
       sum(r.gf) - sum(r.ga) as goal_diff
from teams as t
     join (select host_team_id  as team_id, host_team_score  as gf, guest_team_score as ga
           from matches
           union all
           select guest_team_id, guest_team_score, host_team_score
           from matches) as r
     on r.team_id = t.team_id
group by t.name
order by goal_diff desc, scored desc;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th><th>scored</th><th>conceded</th><th>goal_diff</th></tr><tr><td>Arawali</td><td>9</td><td>5</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>Black Eagles</td><td>14</td><td>12</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>All Stars</td><td>8</td><td>6</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>6</td><td>6</td><td>0</td></tr><tr><td>Rainbow</td><td>13</td><td>14</td><td>-1</td></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>20</td><td>27</td><td>-7</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(6 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> The subquery rewrites every match from both teams' points of view, so each team's goals end up in one column (<code>gf</code>) no matter whether it was home or away. Column names come from the first <code>select</code> of a <code>union</code>. Black Eagles and All Stars tie on goal difference, so the second sort key (<code>scored</code>) decides.</div>
```

### Example 7: Referees in Black Eagles matches

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> List the main referees who have refereed at least one match involving Black Eagles.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: four-table join, in with a list of columns, distinct</div>
```

```sql
select distinct r.name
from referees as r
     join match_referees as mr on mr.referee = r.referee_id
     join matches as m        on m.match_num = mr.match_num
     join teams as t          on t.team_id in (m.host_team_id, m.guest_team_id)
where t.name = 'Black Eagles'
order by r.name;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th></tr><tr><td>Antony Abraham</td></tr><tr><td>Samar Pal</td></tr><tr><td>Sumanta Dutta</td></tr><tr><td>Tony Joseph Louis</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(4 rows)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Join path</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>referees</b></div><span>referee_id</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>match_referees</b></div><span>referee → match_num</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>matches</b></div><span>host / guest team</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>teams</b></div><span>name = Black Eagles</span></div></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> A join condition can be any predicate: <code>t.team_id in (m.host_team_id, m.guest_team_id)</code> matches the team whether it was host or guest. <code>distinct</code> is needed because the same referee can officiate several Black Eagles matches.</div>
```

### Example 8: Teams from cities starting with L

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> List the teams whose city starts with the letter L.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: like, case sensitivity, upper</div>
```

```sql
select name, city from teams where city like 'L%';
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th><th>city</th></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>London</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row) · Thunder's city is stored as 'leeds'</div>
```

```sql
select name, city from teams where upper(city) like 'L%';
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>name</th><th>city</th></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>London</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>leeds</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(2 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> Pattern matching with <code>like</code> is case-sensitive, and the dataset stores one city in lower case. Converting with <code>upper</code> (or <code>lower</code>) before comparing makes the test case-insensitive. PostgreSQL also has <code>ilike</code> for this, but it is not standard SQL.</div>
```

### Example 9: Books issued per department

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> For each department, count the books currently issued to its students. Departments with no issues must still appear.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: chain of left outer joins, count(column) vs count(*)</div>
```

```sql
select d.department_name, count(bi.accession_no) as books_issued
from departments as d
     left join students   as s  on s.department_code = d.department_code
     left join members    as m  on m.roll_no = s.roll_no
     left join book_issue as bi on bi.member_no = m.member_no
group by d.department_name
order by books_issued desc;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>department_name</th><th>books_issued</th></tr><tr><td>Computer Science</td><td>14</td></tr><tr><td>Master Of Computer Application</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>Electrical Engineering</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Mechanical Engineering</td><td>1</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(4 rows)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">⚠️ With count(*) instead</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>department_name</th><th>count(*)</th></tr><tr><td>Computer Science</td><td>16</td></tr><tr><td>Mechanical Engineering</td><td>14</td></tr><tr><td>Electrical Engineering</td><td>12</td></tr><tr><td>Master Of Computer Application</td><td>11</td></tr></table></div><p style="margin:6px 0 0"><code>count(*)</code> also counts the rows the left joins padded with <code>null</code> (students with no book), so it roughly counts students instead of books.</p></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>count(bi.accession_no)</code> counts only real issues. The four departments add up to 20, but <code>book_issue</code> has 21 rows: the 21st book is held by a faculty member (M0060), who has no <code>roll_no</code> and so is not linked to any student.</div>
```

### Example 10: Who in ME has a book?

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Show the name, department and book title for every Mechanical Engineering student who currently has a book issued.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: six-table join, string concatenation</div>
```

```sql
select s.student_fname || ' ' || s.student_lname as student,
       d.department_name, c.title, bi.doi
from book_issue as bi
     join members        as m  on m.member_no     = bi.member_no
     join students       as s  on s.roll_no       = m.roll_no
     join departments    as d  on d.department_code = s.department_code
     join book_copies    as bc on bc.accession_no = bi.accession_no
     join book_catalogue as c  on c.isbn_no       = bc.isbn_no
where d.department_code = 'ME'
order by bi.doi;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>student</th><th>department_name</th><th>title</th><th>doi</th></tr><tr><td>Suresh Singh</td><td>Mechanical Engineering</td><td>Coding For Beginners In Easy Steps</td><td>2021-07-03</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(1 row)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Join path</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>book_issue</b></div><span>member_no, accession_no</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>members → students</b></div><span>roll_no</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>departments</b></div><span>department name</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>book_copies → book_catalogue</b></div><span>title</span></div></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> An issue records a <i>copy</i> (accession number), not a title, so the title needs two hops: copy → ISBN → catalogue. The member number leads to the student through <code>members.roll_no</code>.</div>
```

### Example 11: Titles never issued

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> List the titles of which no copy is currently issued.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: except, in with a subquery</div>
```

```sql
select title
from book_catalogue
where isbn_no in (select isbn_no from book_catalogue
                  except
                  select bc.isbn_no
                  from book_copies as bc
                       join book_issue as bi on bi.accession_no = bc.accession_no)
order by title;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>title</th></tr><tr><td>Basic Computation and Programming with C</td></tr><tr><td>Computer Science Textbook For Class 11</td></tr><tr><td>Computing Fundamentals and C Programming</td></tr><tr><td>Database Management System Oracle SQL</td></tr><tr><td>Excel Vba In Easy Steps</td></tr><tr><td>Machine Learning (in Python and R) For Dummies</td></tr><tr><td>The C Programming Language</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(7 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>all ISBNs except issued ISBNs</code> leaves the ISBNs with no issued copy; the outer query turns them into titles. These are exactly the 7 titles with all 3 copies available in Example 13 (Book availability). The same result can be written with <code>not exists</code> or <code>not in</code> (no nulls here).</div>
```

### Example 12: Authors with more than one book

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Find authors who wrote more than one book in the catalogue.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: group by on two columns, having</div>
```

```sql
select author_fname, author_lname, count(*) as books
from book_authors
group by author_fname, author_lname
having count(*) > 1;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>author_fname</th><th>author_lname</th><th>books</th></tr><tr><td>Mike</td><td>Mcgrath</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Joh Paul</td><td>Mueller</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>E</td><td>Balagurusamy</td><td>2</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(3 rows) · row order may vary</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> An author is identified by first <b>and</b> last name, so both go into <code>group by</code>. Grouping by last name alone would merge different authors who share a surname.</div>
```

## Part B: Views

### Example 13: Book availability

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> For every book title, show how many copies the library owns, how many are issued and how many are available. Save it as a view so the desk staff can query it directly.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: view, join, left outer join, group by, count of a nullable column</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create view book_availability as
select c.isbn_no, c.title,
       count(bc.accession_no)                         as copies,
       count(bi.accession_no)                         as issued,
       count(bc.accession_no) - count(bi.accession_no) as available
from book_catalogue as c
     join book_copies as bc on bc.isbn_no = c.isbn_no
     left join book_issue as bi on bi.accession_no = bc.accession_no
group by c.isbn_no, c.title;

select title, copies, issued, available
from book_availability
order by available, title;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>title</th><th>copies</th><th>issued</th><th>available</th></tr><tr><td>Coding For Beginners In Easy Steps</td><td>3</td><td>3</td><td>0</td></tr><tr><td>Programming in C</td><td>3</td><td>3</td><td>0</td></tr><tr><td>Advanced Database Management System</td><td>3</td><td>2</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Clean Code</td><td>3</td><td>2</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Java 8 Programming Black Book</td><td>3</td><td>2</td><td>1</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">First 5 of 20 rows shown</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">How one title is counted</div><div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>join copies</b></div><span>3 rows: copies A, B, C</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>left join issues</b></div><span>unissued copies get null</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>count(bi.accession_no)</b></div><span>counts only non-null = issued</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>copies − issued</b></div><span>available</span></div></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>count(column)</code> ignores nulls, while <code>count(*)</code> would count every row. The left join keeps copies that were never issued; their <code>bi.accession_no</code> is null, so they are not counted as issued. With an inner join, titles with no issued copies would disappear from the view. Querying the view: <code>select title from book_availability where available = 0;</code> returns the 2 titles with no copy left.</div>
```

### Example 14: Match results

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Create a view that shows each match with the host and guest team names, the score as text and the winner (or "Draw").</div><div class="concept">Concepts: view, joining the same table twice with aliases, case expression, string concatenation ||</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create view match_results as
select m.match_num, m.match_date,
       h.name as host, g.name as guest,
       m.host_team_score || '-' || m.guest_team_score as score,
       case
           when m.host_team_score > m.guest_team_score then h.name
           when m.host_team_score < m.guest_team_score then g.name
           else 'Draw'
       end as winner
from matches as m
     join teams as h on m.host_team_id  = h.team_id
     join teams as g on m.guest_team_id = g.team_id;

select * from match_results order by match_num;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>match_num</th><th>match_date</th><th>host</th><th>guest</th><th>score</th><th>winner</th></tr><tr><td>M0001</td><td>2020-05-06</td><td>Amigos</td><td>Arawali</td><td>5-4</td><td>Amigos</td></tr><tr><td>M0002</td><td>2020-05-07</td><td>Thunder</td><td>All Stars</td><td>0-1</td><td>All Stars</td></tr><tr><td>M0003</td><td>2020-05-09</td><td>Rainbow</td><td>Black Eagles</td><td>2-3</td><td>Black Eagles</td></tr><tr><td>M0004</td><td>2020-05-10</td><td>Black Eagles</td><td>Rainbow</td><td>1-2</td><td>Rainbow</td></tr><tr><td>M0005</td><td>2020-05-11</td><td>All Stars</td><td>Thunder</td><td>2-1</td><td>All Stars</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">First 5 of 16 rows shown</div>
<p>The view can be queried like any table:</p>
```

```sql
select winner, count(*) as matches
from match_results
group by winner
order by matches desc, winner;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>winner</th><th>matches</th></tr><tr><td>Black Eagles</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>Draw</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>All Stars</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Rainbow</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>Arawali</td><td>1</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(7 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>teams</code> appears twice under different aliases: <code>h</code> supplies the host name and <code>g</code> the guest name. The <code>case</code> expression is evaluated for each row. The <code>||</code> operator converts the integer scores to text when it joins them.</div>
```

### Example 15: League table

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Using the <code>match_results</code> view, build a <code>team_standings</code> view with matches played, won, drawn, lost and points (3 for a win, 1 for a draw). Run it in the same transaction as Example 2, so <code>match_results</code> still exists.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: view defined using another view, union all, case inside sum</div>
```

```sql
create view team_standings as
select team,
       count(*)                                           as played,
       sum(case when result = 'W' then 1 else 0 end)      as won,
       sum(case when result = 'D' then 1 else 0 end)      as drawn,
       sum(case when result = 'L' then 1 else 0 end)      as lost,
       sum(case result when 'W' then 3 when 'D' then 1 else 0 end) as points
from (select host as team,
             case when winner = host then 'W'
                  when winner = 'Draw' then 'D' else 'L' end as result
      from match_results
      union all
      select guest,
             case when winner = guest then 'W'
                  when winner = 'Draw' then 'D' else 'L' end
      from match_results) as r
group by team;

select * from team_standings order by points desc, team;
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>team</th><th>played</th><th>won</th><th>drawn</th><th>lost</th><th>points</th></tr><tr><td>Black Eagles</td><td>7</td><td>4</td><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>13</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>6</td><td>2</td><td>2</td><td>2</td><td>8</td></tr><tr><td>All Stars</td><td>3</td><td>2</td><td>1</td><td>0</td><td>7</td></tr><tr><td>Rainbow</td><td>6</td><td>2</td><td>1</td><td>3</td><td>7</td></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>7</td><td>1</td><td>2</td><td>4</td><td>5</td></tr><tr><td>Arawali</td><td>3</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>1</td><td>4</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(6 rows)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Each match becomes two rows, one per team</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>match_results row</th><th>→ rows in r</th></tr><tr><td>M0001 Amigos 5-4 Arawali</td><td>(Amigos, W) and (Arawali, L)</td></tr><tr><td>a 1-1 draw between X and Y</td><td>(X, D) and (Y, D)</td></tr></table></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>team_standings</code> depends directly on <code>match_results</code>, which depends on the base tables. <code>union all</code> (not <code>union</code>) is required: two different matches can produce identical rows such as (Black Eagles, W), and <code>union</code> would remove the duplicates: every team would be left with at most one W, one D and one L, and Black Eagles would show 4 points instead of 13. The points match the <code>team_points</code> function on the Advanced SQL page.</div>
```

### Example 16: CS students only

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Give the CS department office a view of CS students only, through which they can also add new CS students, but never a student of another department.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: updatable view, with check option, not-null columns hidden by a view</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create view cs_students as
select * from students
where department_code = 'CS'
with check option;

insert into cs_students
values ('Asha', 'Rao', 'CS99', 'CS', 'F', '9002000099', '2003-01-15', 'B.Tech');
select count(*) from cs_students;

insert into cs_students
values ('Ravi', 'Kumar', 'ME99', 'ME', 'M', '9002000098', '2003-02-20', 'B.Tech');
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><pre> count
-------
    17

ERROR:  new row violates check option for view "cs_students"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (Ravi, Kumar, ME99, ME, M, 9002000098, 2003-02-20, B.Tech).</pre>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> The view selects from one table with plain columns, so it is updatable. 16 CS students + Asha = 17. Ravi's row would not satisfy <code>department_code = 'CS'</code>, and <code>with check option</code> rejects it.<br><b>Trap:</b> if the view listed only <code>roll_no, student_fname, student_lname, department_code, degree</code>, every insert would fail with <code>null value in column "gender" … violates not-null constraint</code>: columns hidden by a view are filled with null, and every column of <code>students</code> is <code>not null</code>.</div>
```

### Example 17: Issues per member type

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Keep a fast summary of how many books are issued to each member type, and see what happens when a new book is issued.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: materialized view, staleness, refresh</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create materialized view issues_per_type as
select m.member_type, count(*) as books_issued
from book_issue as bi
     join members as m on m.member_no = bi.member_no
group by m.member_type;

select * from issues_per_type order by member_type;
insert into book_issue values ('M0053', '9789351199380C', '2021-08-12');
select * from issues_per_type order by member_type;
refresh materialized view issues_per_type;
select * from issues_per_type order by member_type;
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">The three selects</div><div class="two"><div><div class="flow-label">before and after the insert</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>member_type</th><th>books_issued</th></tr><tr><td>FC</td><td>1</td></tr><tr><td>PG</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>UG</td><td>16</td></tr></table></div></div><div><div class="flow-label">after refresh</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>member_type</th><th>books_issued</th></tr><tr class="hit"><td>FC</td><td><b>2</b></td></tr><tr><td>PG</td><td>4</td></tr><tr><td>UG</td><td>16</td></tr></table></div></div></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> M0053 is a faculty member (FC). The insert changes <code>book_issue</code>, but the materialized view keeps the stored result (FC = 1) until <code>refresh materialized view</code> recomputes it. A normal view would show 2 immediately.</div>
```

```sql
returns integer as $$
```

### Example 19: Books by publisher

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Write a function that takes a publisher name and returns the ISBN, title and year of its books, oldest first.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: table function used in from</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create function books_by_publisher(p varchar)
returns table (isbn_no varchar, title varchar, year integer) as $$
    select c.isbn_no, c.title, c.year
    from book_catalogue as c
    where c.publisher = p
    order by c.year;
$$ language sql;

select * from books_by_publisher('Wiley');
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>isbn_no</th><th>title</th><th>year</th></tr><tr><td>9788126563050</td><td>Machine Learning (in Python and R) For Dummies</td><td>2016</td></tr><tr><td>9788126568932</td><td>Blockchain for Dummies</td><td>2017</td></tr><tr><td>9788126576104</td><td>Artificial Intelligence For Dummies</td><td>2018</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(3 rows)</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> A table function behaves like a parameterised view. Its output columns are named in <code>returns table (…)</code>. Qualifying the columns with <code>c.</code> is optional in a SQL-language function, but in a PL/pgSQL function the output column names become variables, and unqualified column names fail with <code>column reference "isbn_no" is ambiguous</code>. Qualifying them is a safe habit.</div>
```

### Example 20: Student GPA

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Write a function that converts a letter grade to grade points (A+ = 10, A = 9, A- = 8.5, B+ = 8, B = 7, B- = 6.5, C+ = 6, C = 5, C- = 4.5, anything else 0). Use it to compute the credit-weighted GPA of students 1000, 10033 and 10076.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: PL/pgSQL function, case expression, trim, aggregate over a function</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create function grade_points(g varchar)
returns numeric as $$
begin
    return case trim(g)
               when 'A+' then 10  when 'A' then 9  when 'A-' then 8.5
               when 'B+' then 8   when 'B' then 7  when 'B-' then 6.5
               when 'C+' then 6   when 'C' then 5  when 'C-' then 4.5
               else 0
           end;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select s.id, s.name,
       round(sum(c.credits * grade_points(t.grade)) / sum(c.credits), 2) as gpa
from student as s
     join takes  as t on s.id = t.id
     join course as c on c.course_id = t.course_id
where s.id in ('1000', '10033', '10076')
group by s.id, s.name
order by s.id;
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>id</th><th>name</th><th>gpa</th></tr><tr><td>1000</td><td>Manber</td><td>7.03</td></tr><tr><td>10033</td><td>Zelty</td><td>6.68</td></tr><tr><td>10076</td><td>Duan</td><td>8.03</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(3 rows)</div>
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">⚠️ Trap in the dataset: grades with a trailing space</div><p style="margin:0 0 6px">One-letter grades are stored as <code>'A '</code>, <code>'B '</code>, <code>'C '</code> (10011 rows). So:</p><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>query / function</th><th>result</th></tr><tr><td>select count(*) from takes where grade = 'A';</td><td>0</td></tr><tr class="hit"><td>select count(*) from takes where trim(grade) = 'A';</td><td>3318</td></tr><tr><td>grade_points without trim(…), GPA of Zelty</td><td>3.60 (every A, B, C scored 0)</td></tr><tr class="hit"><td>grade_points with trim(…), GPA of Zelty</td><td>6.68</td></tr></table></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> <code>sum(credits × points) / sum(credits)</code> weights each grade by the course credits. <code>trim</code> removes the trailing space so <code>'A '</code> matches <code>'A'</code>.</div>
```

### Example 21: Head-to-head record

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Write a function that, given two team ids, returns how many times each beat the other and how many draws they had, or "never played".</div><div class="concept">Concepts: PL/pgSQL variables, for loop over a query, if / elsif, string building</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create function head_to_head(t1 varchar, t2 varchar)
returns text as $$
declare
    m record;
    w1 integer := 0;  w2 integer := 0;  d integer := 0;
    s1 integer;  s2 integer;
begin
    for m in select * from matches
             where (host_team_id = t1 and guest_team_id = t2)
                or (host_team_id = t2 and guest_team_id = t1)
    loop
        if m.host_team_id = t1 then              -- scores from t1's side
            s1 := m.host_team_score;  s2 := m.guest_team_score;
        else
            s1 := m.guest_team_score; s2 := m.host_team_score;
        end if;
        if s1 > s2 then w1 := w1 + 1;
        elsif s1 < s2 then w2 := w2 + 1;
        else d := d + 1;
        end if;
    end loop;
    if w1 + w2 + d = 0 then
        return 'never played';
    end if;
    return t1 || ' won ' || w1 || ', ' || t2 || ' won ' || w2 || ', drawn ' || d;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select o.name as opponent, head_to_head(t.team_id, o.team_id)
from teams as t, teams as o
where t.team_id = 'T0004' and o.team_id <> t.team_id
order by o.team_id;
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>opponent</th><th>head_to_head</th></tr><tr><td>Amigos</td><td>T0004 won 1, T0001 won 0, drawn 0</td></tr><tr><td>Thunder</td><td>T0004 won 0, T0002 won 1, drawn 1</td></tr><tr><td>Rainbow</td><td>T0004 won 3, T0003 won 1, drawn 0</td></tr><tr><td>All Stars</td><td>never played</td></tr><tr><td>Arawali</td><td>never played</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(5 rows) · Black Eagles (T0004) against every other team</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> The loop visits only matches between the two teams, in either home/away order. The first <code>if</code> turns each match into "t1's goals vs t2's goals", so the second <code>if</code> does not need to care who hosted.</div>
```

### Example 22: Issuing a book safely

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Write a procedure <code>issue_book(member, copy, date)</code> that refuses to issue a copy that is already out, refuses unknown members, enforces the member's quota from the <code>quota</code> table, and otherwise records the issue.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: procedure, select into, several checks, raise exception, raise notice</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create procedure issue_book(m_no varchar, acc_no varchar, issue_date date) as $$
declare
    already   integer;
    holding   integer;
    quota_max integer;
begin
    select count(*) into already from book_issue where accession_no = acc_no;
    if already > 0 then
        raise exception 'copy % is already issued', acc_no;
    end if;

    select q.max_books into quota_max
    from members as m join quota as q on q.member_type = m.member_type
    where m.member_no = m_no;
    if quota_max is null then
        raise exception 'member % does not exist', m_no;
    end if;

    select count(*) into holding from book_issue where member_no = m_no;
    if holding >= quota_max then
        raise exception 'member % already has % books (limit %)', m_no, holding, quota_max;
    end if;

    insert into book_issue values (m_no, acc_no, issue_date);
    raise notice 'issued % to %', acc_no, m_no;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;
```

```{=html}
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Calls, in this order (the 2nd fails because the 1st has just issued that copy)</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>call</th><th>result</th></tr><tr class="hit"><td>call issue_book('M0053', '9789351199380C', '2021-08-12');</td><td>NOTICE: issued 9789351199380C to M0053</td></tr><tr><td>call issue_book('M0054', '9789351199380C', '2021-08-12');</td><td>ERROR: copy 9789351199380C is already issued</td></tr><tr><td>call issue_book('M9999', '9780984782864A', '2021-08-12');</td><td>ERROR: member M9999 does not exist</td></tr></table></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> The checks run in order and <code>raise exception</code> stops the procedure, so nothing is inserted when a check fails. If no member matches, <code>select … into</code> leaves <code>quota_max</code> null, which is how the unknown member is detected. The quota check uses <code>max_books</code> (UG 10, PG 12, FC 15).</div>
```

## Part D: Triggers

### Example 23: No salary cuts

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: university</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Make sure no instructor's salary can ever be reduced, whichever program updates it.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: BEFORE update row trigger, comparing old and new</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create function no_salary_cut() returns trigger as $$
begin
    if new.salary < old.salary then
        raise exception 'salary of % cannot decrease (% -> %)',
                        old.name, old.salary, new.salary;
    end if;
    return new;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger no_salary_cut
before update of salary on instructor
for each row
execute function no_salary_cut();

update instructor set salary = salary * 1.10 where dept_name = 'Biology';
update instructor set salary = salary * 0.90 where dept_name = 'Physics';
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><pre>UPDATE 2
ERROR:  salary of Shuming cannot decrease (108011.81 -&gt; 97210.63)</pre>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> A <code>check</code> constraint only sees the new row, so it cannot compare with the old value; a trigger can. The trigger fires for each row; the first Physics row fails, and because the whole statement is atomic, neither Physics salary changes.</div>
```

### Example 24: One match per team per day

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: flis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> Reject a new match if either team already has a match on that date, or if a team is set to play itself.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: BEFORE insert trigger, exists over other rows, why a check constraint cannot do this</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create function one_match_per_day() returns trigger as $$
begin
    if new.host_team_id = new.guest_team_id then
        raise exception 'a team cannot play itself';
    end if;
    if exists (select * from matches as m
               where m.match_date = new.match_date
                 and (m.host_team_id  in (new.host_team_id, new.guest_team_id)
                   or m.guest_team_id in (new.host_team_id, new.guest_team_id))) then
        raise exception 'a team in match % already plays on %',
                        new.match_num, new.match_date;
    end if;
    return new;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger one_match_per_day
before insert on matches
for each row
execute function one_match_per_day();
```

```{=html}
<div class="panel"><div class="panel-title">Three inserts, tried one at a time</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt "><tr><th>insert into matches values …</th><th>result</th></tr><tr><td>('M0017', '2020-05-06', 'T0002', 'T0006', 0, 0)</td><td>ERROR: a team in match M0017 already plays on 2020-05-06 (Arawali played M0001 that day)</td></tr><tr><td>('M0017', '2020-06-30', 'T0005', 'T0005', 1, 1)</td><td>ERROR: a team cannot play itself</td></tr><tr class="hit"><td>('M0017', '2020-06-30', 'T0005', 'T0006', 2, 2)</td><td>INSERT 0 1</td></tr></table></div></div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> A <code>check</code> constraint can test values within the new row (host ≠ guest), but it cannot query other rows of the table. The trigger runs an <code>exists</code> subquery over the existing matches before the row is stored. Note the parentheses around the two <code>or</code> conditions: without them <code>and</code> binds tighter and the date test would apply to only half of the condition.</div>
```

### Example 25: Logging returned books

```{=html}
<div class="ds">Dataset: lis</div><div class="q"><b>Question.</b> When a book is returned (its row is deleted from <code>book_issue</code>), keep a record of who had it, which copy and when it was issued.</div><div class="concept">Concepts: AFTER delete row trigger, old row, audit table</div>
```

```sql
begin;
create table return_log (member_no    varchar(10),
                         accession_no varchar(20),
                         issued_on    date,
                         returned_on  date default date '2021-08-20');

create function log_return() returns trigger as $$
begin
    insert into return_log(member_no, accession_no, issued_on)
    values (old.member_no, old.accession_no, old.doi);
    return old;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

create trigger log_return
after delete on book_issue
for each row
execute function log_return();

delete from book_issue where member_no = 'M0045';   -- M0045 returns both books
select * from return_log;
select count(*) from book_issue;
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="out-label">Output</div><pre>DELETE 2</pre><div class="out-label">Output</div><div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>member_no</th><th>accession_no</th><th>issued_on</th><th>returned_on</th></tr><tr><td>M0045</td><td>9789332543553C</td><td>2021-08-01</td><td>2021-08-20</td></tr><tr><td>M0045</td><td>9789386551337C</td><td>2021-07-02</td><td>2021-08-20</td></tr></table></div><div class="rows-note">(2 rows) · row order may vary; book_issue now has 19 rows</div>
<div class="why"><b class="t">Why it works.</b> For a delete, only <code>old</code> exists. The row-level trigger fires once per deleted row, so one <code>delete</code> statement removing 2 rows writes 2 log rows. In a real system <code>returned_on</code> would default to <code>current_date</code>; a fixed date is used here so the output is the same every time.</div>
```
